slides.title: Real-World Network Issues
slides.body: Real-World Network Issues

slides.title: From Textbook Networks to the Real World
slides.body:
Introduction
In real networks, internet can slow down, calls can freeze, Wi-Fi can drop, and servers can become unreachable. Network engineers must quickly identify and fix these issues.

slides.title: From Textbook Networks to the Real World
slides.body:
Real-World Problems
Performance problems
The network works, but slowly
High latency
Low throughput
Video buffering
Video calls freezing
Reliability problems
Network connection breaks or becomes unreachable.
Examples: packet loss, connection drops, service not reachable.

slides.title: From Textbook Networks to the Real World
slides.body:
Real-World Problems
Signal problems
The physical signal itself is weak or distorted
A faulty cable
A Wi-Fi dead zone
Electrical interference from a microwave oven

slides.title: Packet Loss
slides.body:
Faulty Network
Packet loss occurs when packets sent from a source fail to reach the destination. In TCP, missing packets are retransmitted, causing delays and reducing network speed

slides.title: Packet Loss
slides.body:
Common Causes
Network congestion
Full router queues lead to dropped packets
Faulty hardware
Damaged cables or failing routers cause packet loss
Wireless interference
Weak Wi-Fi signals drop packets
Software bugs
Misconfigured firewalls or routing loops discard packets

slides.title: Packet Loss
slides.body:
User Impact
How is it measured?
Packet loss is reported as a percentage (e.g., 20% packet loss). The simplest tool is ping. A typical ping output line - ‘5 packets transmitted, 4 received, 20% packet loss’. Anything above 1% is considered a problem for voice and video calls

slides.title: Packet Loss
slides.body:
Troubleshooting Steps
Restart routers and modems
Update drivers and firmware
Replace faulty Ethernet cables
Check for unauthorized or high-traffic devices

slides.title: Signal Problems
slides.body:
Three Impairments
Most "packet loss" actually starts at the physical layer. When a 0 or 1 cannot be cleanly recognised at the receiver, the frame fails the CRC check and is dropped - looking like packet loss to the upper layers. Three impairments cause this:

slides.title: Signal Problems
slides.body:
1
unwanted signal ADDED to the original:
Sources: thermal (random electron motion), crosstalk (leakage between wires), and EMI (motors, microwaves, lights).
Effect: SNR drops → max data rate falls (Shannon)
Three Impairments

slides.title: Signal Problems
slides.body:
Transmitted 
Noise

Noise

slides.title: Signal Problems
slides.body:
2
signal strength LOSS with distance:
Every medium absorbs energy; copper fades faster than fiber
Fix: amplifiers (analog) and repeaters (digital)
Effect: this is why Ethernet on twisted pair is capped at 100 m
Three Impairments

slides.title: Signal Problems
slides.body: Attenuation

slides.title: Signal Problems
slides.body:
3
signal SHAPE changed in transit
Different frequency components travel at slightly different speeds, so a clean square pulse arrives stretched and rounded
Effect: bit boundaries blur and the receiver samples at the wrong moment
Three Impairments

slides.title: Signal Problems
slides.body:
Important Note
In short
Noise adds, Attenuation removes, Distortion reshapes. All three lower the SNR, raise the bit error rate, and surface as packet loss to the upper layers.

slides.title: Repeater and Hub
slides.body:
Layer 1 Devices
1
A signal regenerator:
Works only with bits and has two ports: input and output
Takes a weak signal, cleans it, and retransmits it at full strength
Helps extend cable distance by solving attenuation
Does not check MAC/IP addresses or detect collisions; it only copies bits

slides.title: Repeater and Hub
slides.body:
Repeater
Attenuated Signal
Regenerated Signal
Layer 1 Devices

slides.title: Repeater and Hub
slides.body:
2
A multi-port repeater:
Has many ports (commonly 4, 8, 16, or 24)
When a bit arrives on one port, the hub broadcasts it to every other port. There is no "decision" - every port hears every bit
Half-duplex - a device can either send or receive at a moment, never both. If two devices try to transmit at once, a collision occurs, leading to data loss
Layer 1 Devices

slides.title: Repeater and Hub
slides.body:
Hub
Layer 1 Devices

slides.title: Repeater and Hub
slides.body:
Hubs are obsolete because they broadcast data to all devices, which shares bandwidth .Eg : 100 Mbps ÷ 10 devices ≈ 10 Mbps each – and exposes all transmissions, creating security risks
Switches addressed both issues, replacing hubs in the early 2000s. Repeaters still exist, mostly in long-haul fiber and wireless systems
Layer 1 Devices

slides.title: Switch
slides.body:
Heart of Every Modern LAN
A switch understands frames and MAC addresses. Its job is to receive a frame on one port and forward it to only the port where the destination MAC lives
 It does this using a MAC-to-port mapping called the MAC address table (also called the CAM table)

slides.title: Switch
slides.body:
How A Switch Learns?
When a frame arrives, the switch records the source MAC and port in the MAC table. It then checks the destination MAC:
If the port is known, it forwards the frame to that port (unicast)
01
02
03
If unknown, it floods the frame to all ports until the destination replies
Broadcast frames (FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF) are always flooded, allowing ARP requests to reach all devices

slides.title: Switch
slides.body:
Multicasting By A Switch
Receivers
Sender
Switch

slides.title: Switch
slides.body:
Why Switches Are Better Than Hubs?
Each port is its own collision domain. Two pairs of devices can send and receive at the same time without colliding
01
02
03
04
Full-duplex operation - a device can send and receive simultaneously
Per-port bandwidth - a 24-port gigabit switch gives each port a dedicated 1 Gbps
Security - a frame is sent only to the right port; other devices cannot eavesdrop by default

slides.title: VLANs
slides.body:
Introduction
VLANs
Splitting one switch into many:
A modern switch supports Virtual LANs. The same physical switch is divided into separate logical LANs, isolating traffic. Devices in VLAN 10 cannot directly talk to devices in VLAN 20 even if plugged into the same switch - separation is enforced in hardware.

slides.title: Router
slides.body:
How the Internet Itself Is Built?
A router connects different IP networks/subnets and forwards packets using its routing table
When a packet arrives, it checks the destination IP, applies longest-prefix match, and sends it through the correct next hop/interface
Routing tables are built using static routes or protocols like RIP, OSPF, and BGP

slides.title: Ping
slides.body:
Built on ICMP Echo Request / Reply
The 4-Step Troubleshooting Ladder
ping 127.0.0.1 - Is my own network stack working?
ping 192.168.1.1 - Is my gateway / LAN reachable?
ping 8.8.8.8 - Is the internet up? (no DNS involved)
ping google.com - Is DNS resolving correctly?

slides.title: Ping
slides.body:
Key insight
If Step 3 works but Step 4 fails - the internet is fine, DNS is the problem. This single pattern saves hours of guesswork

slides.title: Reading mdev (Jitter) in Linux Ping Output
slides.body:
Understanding RTT Fluctuation
Linux adds a fourth field to the summary line that Windows does not show:
rtt min/avg/max/mdev = 11.8/12.1/12.4/0.3 ms

slides.title: Reading mdev (Jitter) in Linux Ping Output
slides.body:
Low vs High mdev
Low mdev (e.g. 0.3 ms) = stable, consistent path High mdev (e.g. 67 ms) = jittery link

slides.title: nslookup and netstat - Two More Essential Tools
slides.body:
nslookup - Query the DNS
nslookup queries DNS servers and prints the result. It answers ‘what IP does this domain resolve to?’ and ‘which DNS server gave that answer?’
$ nslookup google.com
Server:    8.8.8.8
Address:   8.8.8.8#53
Name:      google.com
Address:   142.250.183.78

slides.title: nslookup
slides.body:
When nslookup Helps?
‘Site is unreachable by name but works by IP’ → DNS issue
‘Different users see different IPs for the same domain’ → DNS caching or geo-routed DNS
Verifying that a new DNS record has propagated globally

slides.title: netstat
slides.body:
$ netstat -an
$ netstat -tuln
Common states: LISTEN, ESTABLISHED, TIME_WAIT, CLOSE_WAIT
Show Local Network Connections
netstat shows active TCP/UDP connections, open ports, listening processes, and connected remote systems. In modern Linux, ss is commonly used instead
List all connections and listening ports
TCP/UDP listening ports only

slides.title: netstat
slides.body:
When netstat Helps?
‘Is my web server actually listening on port 80?’ → check for LISTEN on :80
‘Why is my app slow on shutdown?’ → many connections in TIME_WAIT
‘Is something already using this port?’ → quick way to find a port conflict
Suspicious activity - too many connections from one IP, or to an unknown remote IP

slides.title: Wireshark
slides.body:
Inspect real packets
Other network commands show summaries, but Wireshark captures actual packets and lets engineers inspect fields, flags, payload, and timing in detail

slides.title: Wireshark
slides.body:
Deep Dive
The full layered breakdown - Ethernet header, IP header, TCP/UDP header, and application payload - all decoded into human-readable fields
Source and destination MAC and IP addresses, port numbers, and packet sizes
TCP flags (SYN, ACK, FIN, RST), sequence and acknowledgement numbers - for diagnosing handshakes and retransmissions 
Inter-packet timing - exact microsecond timestamps to spot delays

slides.title: Wireshark
slides.body: Capture filters vs Display filters

slides.title: Wireshark
slides.body:
Common Things To Check
TCP retransmissions
Wireshark marks them in red; many retransmissions indicate packet loss
TCP three-way handshake
Confirm SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK appear in order
DNS queries and replies
Confirm the right server is being asked and the right answer returned
TLS handshake
Confirm certificate exchange completes and no fatal alerts are sent
1
2
3
4

slides.title: Important
slides.body:
Ethics And Legality:
Capture only on networks the engineer is authorised to monitor. Capturing on a public Wi-Fi or in someone else’s network without permission is illegal in most jurisdictions. Always test in a lab or on a personal home network

slides.title: Case Study 1
slides.body:
The Internet Is Slow
A user says: ‘Yesterday everything was fine. Today, websites take forever, and video calls keep freezing.’ No error messages - just slowness

slides.title: Case Study 1
slides.body:

slides.title: Case Study 1
slides.body:
Always test in layers - local first, then internet IP, then DNS name, then a specific destination
Jitter and loss together usually point to a congested or rerouted link upstream
Half of all ‘slow internet’ complaints are not the user’s network at all - they are an upstream issue

slides.body:
‘Works on my machine’ usually means ‘works on localhost (127.0.0.1)’ - which only confirms the application, not the network
netstat is the fastest way to confirm a service is listening - and on which interface
Three classic blockers between two machines: firewall, NAT, routing. Eliminate them in order
